This message comes from Odoo.
Running a business shouldn't feel like surviving a software group project.
Start managing your business with one unified system.
Odoo is the all-in-one business management software.

It was a spooky week on the stock market, especially for tech investors.
NPR's Scott Horsley reports all of the major market indexes ended the week in the red.
Doubts about artificial intelligence triggered a sell-off for some tech stocks,
even as AI giant Anthropic announced plans to raise up to $100 billion with an initial public offering.
Stock in Google's parent company tumbled after a disappointing earnings report.
Investors continue to pour money into AI data centers, boosting economic growth.
This week, the Commerce Department said GDP grew at an annual rate of 3.4 percent in the third quarter.
Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Worsch welcomed that growth as he and his Fed colleagues held interest rates steady.
For the week, the Dow fell more than eight-tenths of percent, the S&P 500 index fell six-tenths of percent,
and the tech-heavy NASDAQ dropped two percent.
Scott Horsley, NPR News, Washington.
Treasury yields dropped as well as investors searched for more productive ways to invest their money,
even as oil prices rose for the week.
Amid the ongoing war against Iran.
The ICE agent, accused of intentionally running over a man in Houston, Texas, earlier this month,
has been charged with aggravated assault with a deadly weapon.
Cesar Espinosa, with the organization Immigrant Families and Students in the Fight, is demanding justice.
This is not over.
This is just the beginning.
We need there to be an indictment, which already has happened.
We need there to be an arrest, and we need there to be a conviction.
The body cam video shows the ICE agent following the victim Miguel Parra Hernandez as he ran away from the agent,
then allegedly running him over.
Parra Hernandez, who suffered a broken leg, was arrested.
Many U.S. citizens now vote by mail, including one very prominent citizen, Pope Leo.
NPR's Jason DeRose reports on the first pope ever to vote in an American general election.
The Vatican says Pope Leo has exercised his right as a U.S. citizen to vote.
It also says he has done so in the past whenever eligible.
The Vatican press office says that in keeping with this long-standing practice of civic participation,
Leo submitted his mail-in ballot in Chicago, and that he also did so during his years living in Peru,
where he served as a missionary and bishop.
In a statement, the office said, "The Holy Father expresses his belief in the right and duty of citizens to participate in democratic processes."
Pope Leo has both U.S. and Peruvian citizenship.
He's also the Vatican's head of state.
Jason DeRose, NPR News.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky is welcoming U.S. approval of Ukraine's purchase of 500 Patriot interceptors.
The Trump administration announced the approval of the $2.1 billion sale of the Patriot Air Defense equipment
after Ukraine accused the Pentagon of delaying deliveries.
You're listening to NPR.
Today is Halloween, and in case you haven't noticed, the cost of handing out candy isn't getting any cheaper.
NPR's Joe Hernandez reports on the rising cost of chocolate and other Halloween treats.
According to the latest federal data, prices for candy and gum are up 7.7 percent in one year and more than 18 percent in two years.
One major culprit is chocolate, after drought and heavy rains in places like West Africa hurt cocoa harvests in recent seasons.
Global cocoa production is rebounding, but consumer chocolate prices remain elevated, and shoppers are pulling back.
That's according to data from Circana, which tracks sales in supermarkets across the U.S.
They found that people have been buying less chocolate each year for several years running, but dollar sales are up,
which means people are spending more money on chocolate but getting less of it.
Joe Hernandez, NPR News.
Krista Pike has made her first public statement since her botched execution in Tennessee last month.
She says she is in constant pain since surviving a lethal injection.
She added she went into the execution chamber prepared to die in peace, but woke up confused in a hospital bed,
saying she is "deeply hurt by the incompetence."
Pike says she had not contemplated life beyond her execution date and that she is thankful for the medical workers who saved her.
Krista Pike was sentenced to death for the 1995 murder of 19-year-old Colleen Slummer in Knoxville, Tennessee.
Pike was 18 years old at the time of the murder.
I'm Lynda Kenyon, NPR News, in Washington.
